exemplars.response: I claim that mulch reduces soil erosion on a slope. In all three trials, the bare soil lost far more soil than the mulch-covered soil did. exemplars.response: Drought was not the only cause of the Dust Bowl, because the way farmers used the land made the disaster much worse. According to the passage, a long drought began in 1931, but before that, farmers had plowed up about 5 million acres of native prairie grass between 1925 and 1930 to plant wheat. The deep roots of that grass had held the soil in place for thousands of years, so removing it left the ground unprotected. When the dry, loose soil met strong winds, it lifted into the air, and by 1934 government scientists estimated that about 100 million acres of farmland has lost most of their topsoil. Because the dust storms, such as Black Sunday in 1935, began only after both the drought and the plowing, both factors must be blamed.

exemplars.response: Diego should use the Monthly Pass for nine months of the year and switch to Pay Per Ride in the winter. From March through November, he takes about 12 rides a month, so paying per ride would cost 12 × $2.50 = $30, while the pass costs only $18. That saves him $12 every month. In December, January, and February, however, he rides only about 5 times, and 5 × $2.50 = $12.50, which is $5.50 less than the pass. Since Diego can switch plan at the start of any month, he can choose the cheaper option each season. Over a full year, this strategy costs about $199.50, compared with $216 for the pass alone. Therefore, switching plans is the smartest choice.

exemplars.response:
The student council surveyed 94 students at Lincoln Middle School in October and again in January to find out how they travel to school. In October, the school bus was the most common choice, used by 38 students, or about 40 percent. Walking came second with 24 student, and 16 students each traveled by family car or by bike.

By January, the pattern had shifted noticeably. Bus ridership grew from 38 to 46 students, and the number of students dropped off by family car rose from 16 to 24. In contrast, cycling fell sharply from 16 riders to only 3. A likely explanation is that cold, icy weather makes biking uncomfortable, so students choose warmer options. Based on these results, the school might need extra bus capacity during winter months.

The printing press changed life in Europe a lot. Before 1450, all books are copied by hand, so they were rare and expensive. Then Gutenberg invented a press with movable metal letters. This invention changed Europe in two important ways.

exemplars.response:
The invention of the printing press in the 1450s transformed life in Europe by making books common and by helping ideas travel. Before this invention, every book had to be copied by hand, which meant that only churches, universities, and wealthy families could afford them.

One major effect was that books became far cheaper and more plentiful. A scribe might spend months copying a single Bible, but Johannes Gutenberg's press, which used movable metal letters, allowed printers to produce many copies in a fraction of that time. By 1500, presses were operating in more than 200 European cities, and printers had produced about 20 million books. As a result, prices fell and ordinary families could finally buy their own books.

A second effect was that knowledge spread faster and farther. Writers and scientists could publish their discoveries, so readers in distant cities could study, test, and build on them. In addition, because books were easier to find, more people learned to read, and they no longer had to depend entirely of churches and universities for information.

In conclusion, the printing press mattered because it turned books from rare treasures into everyday tools. By spreading knowledge and increasing the number of readers, it helped create a more informed society, which prepared the way for later changes in science and government.

exemplars.response:
On a hot summer afternoon, some parts of a city can feel dramatically hotter than the areas around them. Scientists call this effect an urban heat island. According to the table, a downtown parking lot reached 98°F at 3:00 p.m., while a neighborhood park was only 86°F, a difference of 12 degrees. Two main causes explain why.

The first cause is the dark, hard materials that cover most of a city. Asphalt roads and black roofs absorb most of the sunlight that strikes them and then release the heat slowly, even after sunset. Meanwhile, tall building block breezes that could carry the heat away, and cars and air conditioners add even more heat to the air. This explains why the parking lot, which has asphalt and no trees, was the hottest location.

The second cause is the shortage of plants. Trees provide shade, and their leaves release water vapor that cools the surrounding air in the same way that sweat cools skin. Consequently, the park with grass and many trees was 12 degrees cooler than the parking lot, and the lake shore was cooler still at 83°F.

Cities can reduce this problem by planting more trees, building parks, and painting roofs white. These solutions matter because extreme heat is dangerous for young children, older adults, and outdoor workers. A greener city is therefore a safer one for everyone.

On Tuesday, March 4, our team investigated whether a foam cup keeps water hot longer than a metal cup. We began at 9:50 a.m. by labeling the cups and putting a thermometer in each one. Ten minutes later, at 10:00 a.m., Mr. Okafor poured 200 mL of hot water in both cups, and we recorded the starting temperature: 80 degrees Celsius in each. We then took readings every five minutes. By 10:10 a.m., the foam cup had dropped to 69 degrees while the metal cup had already fallen to 56.

The gap kept growing until the final reading at 10:20 a.m., when the foam cup measured 60 degrees and the metal cup only 43. In other words, the water in the foam cup lost 20 degrees, but the water in the metal cup lost 37. Although the metal cup felt warm on the outside, that warmth showed that heat was escaping through the metal instead of staying with the water. Next time we would repeat the trial three times to be sure that the result is reliable.

annotations.quote: In other words, the water in the foam cup lost 20 degrees, but the water in the metal cup lost 37.
annotations.note: Calculates the change from the log and restates the evidence as a clear comparison.

exemplars.whyThisBand: The recount is organized in clock-time order, uses exact times and quantities as evidence, and calculates the difference between the cups to support the conclusion. Sentence structures vary, with cause, contrast, and concession ('Although'). One preposition slip does not interfere with meaning.
exemplars.nextStep: Keep the calculated evidence and review verbs of pouring and moving, which use 'into' rather than 'in'.
